records.sourceFile: The new challenge of sports nutrition - Accepting insect food as dietary supplements in professional athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Placentino U, Sogari G, Viscecchia R, De Devitiis B, Monacis L. The New Challenge of Sports Nutrition: Accepting Insect Food as Dietary Supplements in Professional Athletes. Foods. 2021;10:1117.
paper.abstract: Sixty-one Italian professional athletes completed a questionnaire on supplement use, nutrition knowledge, food neophobia and willingness to taste and endorse a cricket-flour protein bar. Willingness to taste rose after a short information text, and athletes who were willing to taste were more willing to endorse the product.
paper.tldr: Athletes in this small sample took supplements mainly on the advice of qualified personnel and had weak sports nutrition knowledge. Protein content and curiosity about texture were the main reasons to try an insect bar, while disgust drove refusal.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional questionnaire study of 61 professional athletes recruited on a voluntary basis at the Italian Air Force Sports Centre in Rome. The questionnaire covered supplement use, nutrition knowledge (adapted A-NSKQ), food neophobia (FNS), and willingness to taste and endorse an insect protein bar on a 7-point scale, before and after a short information text. Analysis used descriptive statistics, correlation, regression and repeated-measures tests.
paper.findings: Every athlete reported using supplements; 88.5 percent named qualified personnel as their main information source. Nutrition knowledge was poor (47.8 percent overall). Before the information text, 26 athletes were willing, 7 uncertain and 28 unwilling to taste the bar; willingness rose after the text (z = 4.16, p < 0.001), particularly among unwilling athletes (z = 3.88, p < 0.001). Forty-three athletes (70.5 percent) were classed as tasters. Only 37.7 percent were willing to endorse the bar, and tasters endorsed it more than non-tasters (4.67 vs 2.22, p < 0.001). Men were more willing to endorse than women (4.47 vs 3.3, p = 0.006). Age was positively associated with food neophobia (r = 0.3, p < 0.05).
paper.limitations: The sample is small and convenience-based, from one centre and mainly track and field, fencing and beach volleyball athletes. Willingness was self-reported, and no product was tasted, because the authors could not run a tasting session with insects that might count as hidden substances with a high doping risk. The questionnaire used the FNS rather than an insect-specific attitude scale.
paper.practicalImplications: Any trial of an insect-based protein bar with athletes should lead with its protein content and include clear information, because the authors found that information increased willingness to taste. Endorsement is limited, so do not assume athletes will promote the product. Check anti-doping status before any product is offered, because the authors flag hidden-substance doping risk as the reason they could not run a tasting.
paper.athleteDev: Performance nutrition staff can use these results to frame a novel protein bar around protein content and explain its benefits before asking athletes to try it. The study does not show that the bar supports performance or recovery.
paper.rtp: This study does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport and should not be used to set nutrition plans for injured athletes.

records.sourceFile: The potential role of nutrition in overtraining syndrome - A narrative review.pdf

paper.citation: la Torre ME, Monda A, Messina A, de Stefano MI, Monda V, Moscatelli F, et al. The Potential Role of Nutrition in Overtraining Syndrome: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2023;15:4916.
paper.abstract: Overtraining syndrome follows a prolonged period of overreaching with inadequate recovery, and is linked to systemic inflammation and central nervous system effects. This narrative review examines how diet and nutrition can influence overtraining syndrome, from prevention to treatment.
paper.tldr: Poor or unbalanced nutrition can worsen overtraining and slow recovery, so energy, carbohydrate, protein, fat and micronutrient intake matter for athletes under heavy load. The evidence for specific supplements against overtraining is limited and mixed.
paper.methods: Narrative review. The authors state a non-systematic approach to collecting and analysing articles; no search strategy or inclusion criteria are reported.
paper.findings: The review summarises the main hypotheses for overtraining syndrome (cytokine, glutamine, central fatigue, glycogen, autonomic and oxidative stress) and states that inadequate energy, carbohydrate, protein, fat, fluid or micronutrient intake can aggravate fatigue and recovery problems. It describes BCAA and high-dose antioxidant results as inconsistent or inconclusive, presents ketone esters favourably based on limited studies, and calls for more research on creatine and MCTs.
paper.limitations: The authors state that the non-systematic selection may introduce selection error and call for systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Evidence on nutrition in overtraining is sparse, several claims rest on animal or mechanistic studies, and prevalence data are lacking.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes in heavy training should match energy and carbohydrate intake to load and meet protein, fluid and micronutrient needs. The review suggests that markers such as post-exercise lactate or heart rate variability could help identify overtraining, but it does not validate them for diagnosis.
paper.athleteDev: Match carbohydrate, protein and fluid intake to training load and watch recovery, since poor intake can slow recovery and compound fatigue. Supplements such as BCAAs or antioxidants should not be treated as a fix for overtraining.
paper.rtp: This review addresses overtraining and recovery nutrition in athletes in general. It does not give return-to-sport criteria after injury and cannot be used for return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Thermoregulation, Fluid Balance,        and Sweat Losses in American Football Players.pdf

paper.citation: Davis JK, Baker LB, Barnes K, Ungaro C, Stofan J. Thermoregulation, Fluid Balance, and Sweat Losses in American Football Players. Sports Medicine. 2016;46:1391-1405.
paper.abstract: A review of laboratory and field studies on thermoregulation, fluid balance and sweat losses in American football players. It covers heat illness rates, body size and uniform effects, sweating rates by age and level, mild fluid losses, and sweat sodium.
paper.tldr: Football players, especially larger linemen, sweat heavily and face higher heat illness risk during preseason practice, while fluid losses are usually mild. Staff should monitor large players closely in the first three to four days of practice.
paper.methods: Review of laboratory and field studies, using a described search of PubMed and EBSCO from inception to January 2016, reference-list checks and broad inclusion criteria (English, peer-reviewed, healthy youth and adult athletes). No pooled analysis or formal quality scoring is reported.
paper.findings: Heat illness and heat stroke are more common in football than in other sports, and most cases occur in preseason practice. Linemen have higher body mass and body fat, lower surface area to mass ratios and lower aerobic capacity, and show higher core temperatures and sweating rates than backs. Full or partial uniforms raise sweating rates compared with shorts, with no difference between full and half pads; sweat sodium concentration is similar to other sports, and mean body mass loss in most field studies was about 2% or less.
paper.limitations: Most field studies are from the northeastern U.S. and few quantified exercise intensity. Few studies have examined high school players or hot southern regions. Long-term outcomes and the sodium replacement needed for performance are not known.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should monitor players, particularly large linemen, closely during the first three to four days of preseason practice. Individual sweat rates and body mass changes can guide fluid plans, with the aim of avoiding both over-drinking (body mass gain) and under-drinking (body mass loss of 3% or more).
paper.athleteDev: Youth players sweat less than adults and have lower sweat sodium, so heat strain and fluid needs differ with age and maturation. The review does not show that heat management changes development or performance outcomes in young players.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return to sport or injury. It can inform heat acclimatization planning in general, but it cannot show that any heat or fluid strategy shortens return-to-play timelines or reduces re-injury.

records.sourceFile: Tirzepatide in Sport - A comprehensive review of its metaoblic impacts and potential applications for athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Biesiada W, Kopczyńska E, Kulej P, Woźniak J, Kmieć JW, Chernysh AM, et al. Tirzepatide in Sport: A Comprehensive Review of its Metabolic Impacts and Potential Applications for Athletes. Quality in Sport. 2025;37:57025.
paper.abstract: Tirzepatide is a GIP and GLP-1 receptor dual agonist used for type 2 diabetes and obesity. This review examines its pharmacology, its effects on body composition, its possible use by athletes in endurance, strength and recovery, and the ethical and anti-doping questions it raises. The authors judge the athletic benefits promising but unproven and call for more research, especially on long-term effects on performance and muscle mass in healthy people.
paper.tldr: The review suggests tirzepatide could support body-composition goals and recovery in athletes, but it cites no athlete trials. Any athletic use would need medical oversight and anti-doping review before it is considered.
paper.methods: Narrative review of literature from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase and Google Scholar, using search terms on tirzepatide, GLP-1/GIP agonism, metabolic therapy, sports performance, body composition, endurance and recovery. No inclusion criteria or systematic selection process are reported.
paper.findings: The authors describe large weight and fat loss in trials of people with obesity or type 2 diabetes, and argue from mechanism and preclinical work that lean mass may be preserved. They also propose anti-inflammatory and glycogen-sparing effects that could help endurance and recovery. These are presented as hypotheses, not as effects tested in athletes.
paper.limitations: The review reports no inclusion criteria, selection process or quality appraisal. Most cited evidence comes from people with type 2 diabetes or obesity, and some mechanisms, such as stimulation of mitochondrial biogenesis and lean-mass preservation, are stated as established without athlete data.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes and staff should not treat tirzepatide as a performance aid on the basis of this review. Any use would need medical oversight, a check of WADA status at the time, and attention to the gastrointestinal side effects and hypoglycemia risk the authors list for unsupervised use.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The review shows no tested performance effect in athletes. It is useful only as background for a medical and anti-doping review when an athlete asks about tirzepatide, and it does not support changes to training or nutrition plans.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Cannot inform return to sport. The review does not study injured athletes or rehabilitation and should not guide return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Topical sodium bicarbonate - No improvement in blood buffering capacity or exercise performance.pdf

paper.citation: McKay AKA, Peeling P, Binnie MJ, Goods PSR, Sim M, Cross R, et al. Topical Sodium Bicarbonate: No Improvement in Blood Buffering Capacity or Exercise Performance. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2020 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: The study assessed a topical sodium bicarbonate lotion on blood buffering capacity and performance in recreationally active participants (study A) and moderately trained athletes (study B). In study A, the lotion did not raise pH or bicarbonate, while oral bicarbonate did, and cycling time to exhaustion did not differ (349 vs 363 s). In study B, the lotion did not change blood parameters, mean power or peak power. The authors conclude the lotion was ineffective in altering buffering capacity or enhancing performance.
paper.tldr: A bicarbonate lotion applied to the legs did not raise blood buffering or improve sprint or time-to-exhaustion performance in these tests, while oral bicarbonate did raise blood buffering. Athletes should not use this lotion in place of oral bicarbonate on the basis of this study.
paper.methods: Study A: 10 recreationally active adults (7 men, 3 women) completed two counterbalanced double-blind trials of 30-second cycling efforts at 120% peak power to exhaustion, after either oral bicarbonate (0.3 g/kg) with placebo lotion or the lotion with an oral placebo. Blood was sampled over 90 minutes and after exercise. Study B: 10 moderately trained male cyclists and triathletes completed three 30-second Wingate sprints 30 minutes after either the lotion or a placebo lotion, in a randomized, double-blind design.
paper.findings: In study A, oral bicarbonate raised blood bicarbonate and pH at rest and during recovery, while the lotion did not. Time to exhaustion was 363 s with oral bicarbonate and 349 s with the lotion (P = .697), GI symptoms did not differ, and perceived exertion was slightly higher in the lotion trial (18.9 vs 18.3). In study B, mean and peak power did not differ between the lotion and placebo (P = .108 and P = .448).
paper.limitations: Small samples, one product and one matched dose. The results and discussion report different bicarbonate rises for oral dosing at 90 minutes (4.7 vs 6.5 mmol/L), and the senior author accepted a scientific advisory board role with the product's company during peer review.
paper.practicalImplications: The lotion did not change blood buffering at a dose matched to 0.3 g/kg oral bicarbonate, so the authors advise oral rather than topical bicarbonate. Oral bicarbonate did not improve performance in Study A either, so this study does not itself show an oral benefit, and the authors recommend trialling any bicarbonate protocol before competition.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Do not use this lotion as a substitute for oral bicarbonate for sprint or time-to-exhaustion performance. Athletes who use oral bicarbonate should trial their protocol before competition, as the authors note large individual variation in response.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Cannot inform return to sport. The participants were healthy adults and trained athletes, and the study did not assess injured or recovering athletes.

records.sourceFile: Training load and carbohydrate periodization practices of elite male Australian football players - Evidence of fueling for the work required.pdf

paper.citation: Routledge HE, Graham S, Di Michele R, Burgess D, Erskine RM, Close GL, Morton JP. Training Load and Carbohydrate Periodization Practices of Elite Male Australian Football Players: Evidence of Fueling for the Work Required. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2020;30(4):280-286.
paper.abstract: In 42 professional Australian football players over two in-season microcycles, GPS load was highest on game day and self-reported carbohydrate intake varied across the week, peaking the day before games. Carbohydrate intake during games was much higher than during training, mostly from fluids, but the authors conclude that the reported intakes are low and probably underreported.
paper.tldr: Australian football players appear to vary carbohydrate intake with the weekly training load, eating most the day before a game. Their reported intakes are still low for the workload, and the carbohydrate recalls are probably underestimates.
paper.methods: Forty-two players were studied across a home and an away microcycle in the 2017 season. GPS (Optimeye S5, 10 Hz) recorded total distance, running, high-speed running and sprinting. Daily carbohydrate intake was estimated from 4-day food diaries, 24-hour recall and remote food photography, with in-game and in-training intake recalled within 30 minutes. Repeated-measures general linear models were used for day and fixture week.
paper.findings: Total distance was greater on game day (13 km) than on all training days. Self-reported daily carbohydrate was lowest on GD-3 (1.5 g/kg home, 1.4 g/kg away) and highest on GD-1 (4.3 g/kg home, 4.8 g/kg away). During games, players consumed 59 ± 19 g of carbohydrate (34 ± 11 g/h), more from fluids than gels (38 ± 18 g vs 22 ± 20 g), while training intake was 1 ± 1 g. Fifty-three percent of players reached the 30 to 60 g/h range during games.
paper.limitations: Intake was self-reported and probably underestimated, and the authors could not separate deliberate from habitual choices. The sample is one club over two microcycles, and game-day carbohydrate data came from 22 games. The abstract gives daily intakes of 1.8, 1.4, 2.5 and 4.5 g/kg, which do not match Table 2 (for example 2.1 and 1.8 g/kg on GD-4), the abstract says 75% of game carbohydrate came from fluids while the results give 38 g fluids vs 22 g gels (about 63%), and the abstract places the monitored training session 4 days before games while the methods say 2 days (GD-2).
paper.practicalImplications: Players may need education on carbohydrate needs on training days and on high-load days before games, not only on the day before a match. Match intake of 30 to 60 g/h is achievable with fluids and gels, and the authors suggest that intake should be checked with methods more accurate than recall.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Plan carbohydrate intake around the weekly load, so that high-load training days get more fuel than the current pattern suggests, and build match-day intake toward 30 to 60 g/h with fluids or gels. Use a more objective method than recall when monitoring intake, since self-report probably understates it.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It studied in-season intake and GPS load in players and included no injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes.
